notes.meaning: News of Israel's victories at Jericho and Ai spread across western Canaan, from the hill country down to the Mediterranean coast. The kings of these different peoples put aside their own rivalries and united to fight Joshua and Israel. Their fear drove them to band together in a doomed war against the Lord's people.

Gibeon was an important royal city north of Jerusalem, inhabited by Hivites. When the Gibeonites heard how Israel completely destroyed Jericho and Ai, they realized they could not win by force. Instead of joining the military alliance against Israel, they decided to try another way to survive.

The Gibeonites sent a delegation pretending to be messengers from a distant nation. They loaded their donkeys with old, frayed sacks and cracked leather wineskins that had been patched together. This clever disguise was meant to prove that they had been traveling on the road for many weeks.

The messengers wore patched sandals and ragged clothes to look like weary travelers from a far-off land. They also packed bread that was dry, crumbly, and moldy. Every detail of their appearance was planned to deceive the senses of the Israelite leaders.

The envoys arrived at Israel's camp at Gilgal and asked Joshua and the leaders to make a treaty with them. Under God's law, Israel was permitted to make peace treaties with distant nations, but was commanded to destroy the peoples living in the land of Canaan. The Gibeonites pretended to come from afar so they could secure this protection.

Israel's leaders immediately suspected that these visitors might actually be local Canaanites. They warned them that God's law strictly forbade Israel from making covenants with people living in the land. Even though they noticed the danger, the leaders did not investigate carefully enough.

The Gibeonites humbly presented themselves as servants, offering to submit on whatever terms Joshua gave them. Joshua pushed for specifics and asked who they were and where they had come from. Their polite submission was an attempt to dodge the question and win Israel's goodwill.

The messengers repeated that they came from a very distant country and claimed they had traveled because of the fame of the Lord. They spoke with reverence about the miracles God did in Egypt during the Exodus. By praising Israel's God, they flattered the leaders and made their story sound deeply sincere.

differ.view: Some see their words as a clever pretence of faith, designed only to save their skins through deceit.
Others see a sincere fear of God and a genuine desire to cast themselves on His mercy beneath their trickery.

notes.meaning: The envoys mentioned Israel's victories over the Amorite kings Sihon and Og on the east side of the Jordan River. They cleverly left out recent events like the crossing of the Jordan and the fall of Jericho and Ai. Mentioning recent local battles would have proven they lived close enough to hear current news.

differ.view: Some see their words as a clever pretence of faith, designed only to save their skins through deceit.
Others see a sincere fear of God and a genuine desire to cast themselves on His mercy beneath their trickery.

notes.meaning: The messengers claimed that their elders and citizens had sent them on this long trip to seek peace. Gibeon was governed by a council of elders rather than a king, which gave their official embassy an air of dignity. They asked to become Israel's servants in exchange for a binding covenant of peace.

The envoys held up their bread as physical proof of their story, claiming it was warm from the oven on the day they left home. Now, they pointed out, it was dry, crumbly, and covered in mold. They offered this visible evidence to settle any doubts about how long they had been traveling.

The men showed their cracked leather wineskins and their ragged clothes and sandals as further evidence. They insisted that all this wear and tear came from a grueling, long-distance journey. They built a convincing case using items that anyone could see and touch.

Israel's leaders examined the provisions and accepted the evidence of their own eyes, but they failed to pray and seek the Lord's guidance. God had provided the high priest with the Urim and Thummim to reveal His will, but the leaders relied on human judgment instead. Walking by sight rather than by faith led them straight into a trap.

Joshua agreed to a peace treaty that guaranteed the Gibeonites would not be put to death, and the tribal leaders confirmed it with a solemn oath. Making a covenant in the ancient world involved sacred vows and sacrifices before the Lord. Because the oath was sworn in God's name, it became completely binding on Israel.

differ.view: Others teach that God's command to destroy the Canaanites was directed at those who stubbornly resisted, so the oath to spare those who surrendered was lawful and binding.

notes.meaning: Just three days after swearing the oath, the Israelites learned that the Gibeonites were actually near neighbors living right in Canaan. Gilgal was only about a day's march from Gibeon, so the truth was quickly uncovered. Israel's careless haste was rewarded with public shame and embarrassment.

Israel's troops marched into the territory of Gibeon and reached its four allied cities on the third day. These cities—Gibeon, Chephirah, Beeroth, and Kiriath-jearim—formed a local league of Hivite settlements. One of them, Kiriath-jearim, would later hold the sacred Ark of the Covenant for many years.

The Israelite army refrained from attacking the cities because their leaders had sworn a sacred oath by the Lord, the God of Israel. When the rest of the people realized they could not take the cities or their plunder, they complained bitterly against the leaders. The congregation was angry both at missing the spoils of war and at the foolish blunder their rulers had made.

The rulers stood firm and explained that they could not harm the Gibeonites because they had sworn an oath by the name of the Lord. Even though the treaty was won by trickery, breaking a vow made in God's name would dishonor the Lord Himself. God's people were required to keep their promises, even when keeping them caused personal trouble or loss.

The leaders decided to spare the lives of the Gibeonites so that God's anger would not strike Israel for breaking a sacred oath. Breaking a covenant sworn in the Lord's name invited divine judgment on the whole nation. Keeping their sworn word was the only way to protect Israel from God's wrath.

The leaders proposed that while the Gibeonites would be allowed to live, they would be reduced to perpetual public servitude as woodcutters and water carriers. This heavy physical labor supplied fuel for the sacrifices and water for the community and tabernacle. This compromise honored the oath to spare their lives while punishing their deception and pacifying the angry congregation.

Joshua called the Gibeonites before him and directly confronted them about their dishonesty. He demanded to know why they had lied about coming from a faraway country when they actually lived right among them. By questioning them publicly, Joshua made it clear that trickery could not go unaddressed.

Joshua pronounced a curse on them, sentencing them and their descendants to unending service as woodcutters and water carriers for God's sanctuary. This judgment fulfilled the ancient curse of servitude spoken over Canaan, reducing them from free citizens to humble laborers. At the same time, it brought them into regular proximity to the worship of the true God.

The Gibeonites confessed that they acted out of overwhelming fear because they knew God had commanded Moses to give Israel the entire land and wipe out its inhabitants. They genuinely believed that the Lord would keep His promises and destroy Canaanite resistance. Their fear of God's power drove them to lie, because they saw no other hope of staying alive.

The Gibeonites placed themselves entirely at Joshua's mercy, telling him to do whatever seemed good and right. They did not argue against their demotion to servants or make excuses for their deceit. They willingly surrendered their freedom just to preserve their lives.

Joshua protected the Gibeonites from the angry Israelites who wanted to execute them, ensuring that not one of them was killed. He balanced justice and mercy by sparing their lives according to the oath while holding them to their required service. Joshua showed true leadership by honoring a solemn commitment even in difficult circumstances.

On that day, Joshua formally assigned the Gibeonites to cut wood and draw water for the congregation and for the Lord's altar, at whatever place God would choose for His sanctuary. They faithfully carried out these duties for generations, supporting the tabernacle and later the temple. Though brought in through deception, they remained under the protection of God's covenant and served at His house.
